author_read_locators.locator: §1.1.3, PDF pp.39–40 (printed pp.31–32), Schmidt decompositions; §§2.1.2–2.1.3, PDF pp.69–80 (printed pp.61–72), states, ensembles, partial trace and purifications; §2.3.1, PDF pp.109–110 (printed pp.101–102), finite positive measurement families.

item_dispositions.detail: §2.1.2 identifies density operators as positive semidefinite trace-one operators; the local definition also defines support and faithfulness and excludes the zero space.
§2.3.1 defines a finite family of positive measurement operators summing to identity; the local definition states the underlying algebraic data without adopting a measurement law.
§2.1.2 identifies pure states with normalized rank-one projectors and vectors modulo unit phase; the local definition uses the repository linear-first convention.
From the positive-family identity in §2.3.1, the complement of a member is the sum of the other positive terms; the finite-sum proof, including one outcome, is local.
§2.1.2 gives the completely mixed state I/d; the local proof verifies positivity and trace for every nonzero finite-dimensional H.
§2.1.2 relates unit vectors modulo phase to rank-one projectors; the local proof establishes both directions, positivity, and trace.
§1.1.3 derives Schmidt form from the singular value decomposition; the local proof fixes the second-factor conjugation for the repository convention.
§§2.1.2–2.1.3 define finite state ensembles and vector purifications; the local definition fixes zero-weight components and finite auxiliary spaces.
§2.1.2 gives the spectral mixture of a density operator; the local proof omits zero eigenvalues and identifies the number of terms with rank.
§2.1.2 states convex combinations of density operators remain density operators; the local proof includes zero weights and block regrouping.
The source develops finite ensembles, effects, and purifications; its statements do not supply the grouped mixed-component square-root-filter identity, which is proved locally.
§2.1.3, Theorems 2.10–2.12, gives the rank criterion and unitary equivalence; the local proof handles arbitrary specified embeddings and repeated eigenvalues.
§2.1.2 identifies pure states with rank-one density operators; the local proof normalizes the unique spectral weight and proves ray uniqueness.
§2.1.2 states convexity of density operators; the local proof proves positivity and trace via the finite barycenter supplier.
Theorem 2.10 gives the rank threshold for purification; the local proof derives the lower bound for every finite auxiliary space and attains it.

sources.title: John Preskill, Quantum Computation, Chapter 2: Foundations I: States and Ensembles (updated July 2015)

author_read_locators.locator: §2.3, printed pp.16–22 (density operators and reductions); §2.4, printed pp.23–25 (Schmidt decomposition); §§2.5.1–2.5.2 and §2.5.5, printed pp.27–36 (convexity, ensembles, purifications and HJW).

item_dispositions.detail: §2.3 defines subsystem density operators and partial-trace reductions; local scope excludes physical postulates.
§2.3 distinguishes pure states from mixed density operators and records phase-equivalent unit representatives.
§2.3 gives normalized density operators, including a maximally mixed example; the general I/d verification is local.
§2.3 explains phase invariance of the rank-one projector; injectivity and the full bijection are proved locally.
§2.4 derives Schmidt form for a bipartite pure state and relates the coefficients to singular values.
§§2.5.1–2.5.2 and §2.5.5 describe ensembles and purifications; the local definition fixes finite and zero-weight conventions.
§2.5.1 uses diagonalization to express density operators as convex sums of pure states; zero eigenvalues are omitted locally.
§2.5.1 proves convexity and §2.5.2 discusses ensemble averages; the local proof also treats zero-total blocks.
§2.5.5 proves the HJW correspondence for pure-state ensembles; the local argument proves the stronger grouped mixed-component identity for arbitrary purifications.
§2.5.5 relates purifications of the same density operator by an auxiliary unitary; the local proof handles arbitrary dimensions and embeddings.
§2.3 identifies pure projectors; the local proof derives the rank-one converse with its trace normalization.
§2.5.1 explicitly proves convexity, including endpoint parameters in the local proof.
§2.5.5 gives the dimension-r purification route; the local proof supplies the lower bound for all finite auxiliary spaces.

item_dispositions.detail: §15.1 defines mixed states by positive semidefinite trace-one density matrices.
§15.1 defines POVM elements as positive semidefinite matrices with finite sum I; the local definition makes no outcome-law assertion.
§15.1 identifies pure states with rank-one outer products; the local definition makes the ray quotient and root convention explicit.
The POVM positivity and completeness condition in §15.1 supplies the interface; the complement-positive finite-sum proof is local.
§15.1 uses normalized density matrices; the all-dimension I/d construction and proof are local.
§15.1 identifies pure states as rank-one density matrices; the local proof supplies the exact ray/projector bijection.
§18.3 states Schmidt form and derives it using the reduced density matrix; the local proof instead uses matrix SVD with the root convention.
§15.1 defines mixtures and §18.3 Exercise 4 defines purification by partial trace.
§15.1 records the diagonalization route to an orthogonal pure-state mixture; the local proof states the finite spectral argument.
§15.1 treats positive mixtures of states; linearity, zero weights, and block regrouping are proved locally.
§15.1 and §18.3 supply mixture, effect, and purification context; the mixed-component filter identity is proved locally.
§18.3 Exercise 4(b)–(c) asks for rank-bounded purification and unitary equivalence; the local proof resolves both for arbitrary finite auxiliary spaces.
§15.1 states pure iff rank one; the local proof adds the unique-ray statement.
§15.1 uses density-matrix mixtures; the local proof supplies the segment argument and endpoint cases.
§18.3 Exercise 4(b) gives the rank-r purification bound; Watrous Theorem 2.10 is the direct rank-threshold treatment, and the local proof gives the matching lower bound.
